before: Wretched one, do you really rank pleasure above goods so many and so great? I understand your postponement, even if you cover it over with words. The facts themselves cry out, even if your voice is silent. "Let me use my flesh for the enjoyment of shameful things; let me wallow in the mire of pleasures; let me stain my hands with blood, take what belongs to others, walk in deceit, swear falsely, lie—and then, when I finally stop doing evil, I will receive baptism." If sin is good, then keep it to the end. But if it harms the one who does it, why do you persist in what destroys you? No one who wants to vomit up bile first gathers more of it into himself through a bad and dissolute diet. You should cleanse the body of what troubles it, not make the disease greater than your strength. A ship shows how much weight of cargo it can bear; anything beyond that sinks it. Be afraid that you may suffer the same thing—that by making your sins greater than the forgiveness, you may suffer shipwreck before the hoped-for harbor. Does God not see what happens? Does He not understand your thoughts? Does He cooperate with you in your lawless deeds? You thought that I would be just like you, He says (Psalm 49:21). When you seek the friendship of a mortal man, you win him over with good deeds, saying and doing the things you know please him. But when you are drawing near to God and hoping to be received into the rank of a son, you do what is hostile to God and dishonor Him by breaking the law—and from the very things that most offend Him, you hope for closeness? Watch out: if you pile up a mass of evils for yourself in hope of redemption, you may gather sin and yet miss the forgiveness. God is not mocked (Galatians 6:7). Do not trade in the grace. Do not say, "The law is good, but sin is sweeter." Pleasure is the devil's fishhook, dragging you to destruction. Pleasure is the mother of sin, and sin is the sting of death (1 Corinthians 15:56). Pleasure is the nurse of the eternal worm: for a time it soothes the one who enjoys it, but afterward it produces a bitterness sharper than gall. Your postponement cries out nothing other than this: "Let sin reign in me first, and then one day the Lord will reign. Let me present my members as weapons of unrighteousness to lawlessness, and then one day I will present them as weapons of righteousness to God." That is how Cain offered his sacrifices: the first things to his own enjoyment, the second to God who created and gave them. While you are strong in deeds, you spend your youth on sins. When your organs are worn out, then you bring them to God—when they are good for nothing, when they must lie idle because their strength has been paralyzed by the decay of time. Self-control in old age is not self-control; it is inability for licentiousness. A corpse is not crowned. No one is righteous merely through being unable to do evil. As long as you have strength, master sin by your will. For this is virtue: turning away from evil and doing good. But mere inactivity in wickedness deserves neither praise nor punishment on its own. If you stop sinning because of age, the credit belongs to weakness. We praise those who are good by choice, not those who are kept from evil by some necessity.

before: But since not only forgiveness of the past has been proclaimed beforehand, but also gifts of the future, you are wronging yourself in ways not even one of your enemies would have spitefully done to you, and yet you think you have planned well and reasoned profitably about yourself. You refuse the forgiveness and die in your debts. And you know this: the debtor of ten thousand talents would have received forgiveness, if he had not renewed the demand for payment against himself by his cruelty toward his fellow servant (Matthew 18:23-35). We must be careful not to suffer the same thing once we have received grace, by not forgiving our own debtors, so that the gift may remain secure for us.

Enter the inner chamber of your soul, and stir up the memory of what you have done. If your sins are many, do not be discouraged by their number. For where sin increased, grace increased all the more (Romans 5:20), if you accept the grace. The one who owes much will have much forgiven, so that he may love more (Luke 7:47). But if your sins are small and trivial, and not leading to death, why are you anxious about the future, when you bore the past not ignobly, and that without yet being trained by the law?

Now consider your soul as standing on a balance, pulled from one side by angels and from the other by demons. To which will you give the weight of your heart? What will win in you: pleasure of the flesh, or holiness of the soul? Enjoyment of present things, or desire for the things to come? Will angels receive you, or will those who hold you keep their grip?

In battle, generals distribute a watchword to their troops, so that friends can easily call to one another, and so that when they are mixed with the enemy in close combat, the separation can be clearly made. No one will recognize whether you are one of ours or one of the enemy, unless you show your allegiance through the mystical symbols, unless the light of the Lord's face is marked upon you (Numbers 6:25). How will the angel claim you? How will he snatch you from the enemy, if he does not recognize the seal? How will you say, "I belong to God," if you do not carry the marks of identification?

Or do you not know that the destroyer passed over the houses that were sealed, but in the unsealed houses he slaughtered the firstborn (Exodus 12:23)? An unsealed treasure is easy prey for thieves; an unmarked sheep is plotted against without risk.

Are you young? Secure your youth with the bridle of baptism. Has your prime passed? Do not be deprived of the provisions for the journey; do not lose the amulet; do not think about the eleventh hour as if it were the first. For it is fitting even for the one beginning life to keep the end before his eyes.

If one of the doctors promised you that by some devices and contrivances he would make you young from old, would you not long for that day to come, when you were about to see yourself returning to your prime? But when baptism promises to make your soul flourish again—the soul you have made old, and which it promises to rescue from lawlessness, though you have shown it stained—you despise your benefactor and do not run to the promise.

Do you not desire to see what the great wonder of the promise is? How is a person reborn without a mother? How does the one who is growing old and being corrupted according to the desires of deceit become vigorous again, and return to youth, and come back to the true flower of young manhood?

Baptism is ransom for captives, forgiveness of debts, death of sin, regeneration of the soul, a garment of light, a seal that cannot be assailed, a vehicle to heaven, the means of gaining the kingdom, the gift of adoption.

before: The wise Solomon, dividing up the times of life's affairs and setting aside the right moment for each thing that happens, said: "There is a time for everything, and a season for every matter: a time to be born, and a time to die" (Ecclesiastes 3:1-2). But I would alter the wise man's saying just a little, and proclaim to you the saving message: there is a time to die, and a time to be born.

Why this change? Because he was speaking about things that come into being and pass away, following bodily nature, and so he placed birth before death—for no one can experience death without first being born. But I am about to speak of spiritual rebirth, and so I place death before life. For by dying to the flesh we gain birth in the Spirit, as the Lord also says: "I kill, and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39). Let us die, then, so that we may live. Let us put to death the sinful nature, which cannot submit to God's law, so that the mindset of the Spirit may grow strong in us—the mindset through which life and peace naturally come. Let us be buried with Christ, who died for us, so that we may also rise with Him who secured our resurrection.

Different times suit different things: there is a time for sleep and a time for waking, a time for war and a time for peace. But for baptism, the entire life of human beings is the time. A body cannot live without breathing, and a soul cannot hold together without knowing its Creator. Ignorance of God is the death of the soul. And the unbaptized person has not been enlightened. Without light, an eye cannot see what belongs to it, nor can a soul receive the contemplation of God.

Every moment, then, offers the opportunity for salvation through baptism—whether you name night or day, an hour or an instant, or the very briefest point of time. But surely the moment most closely related to baptism is the most fitting. What could be more akin to baptism than the day of Easter? That day is the memorial of the resurrection, and baptism is the power that leads to resurrection. On the day of resurrection, then, let us receive the grace of the resurrection. This is why the Church calls her nurslings together from afar with a loud proclamation, so that those for whom she long labored in birth she may bring forth on that day—and having weaned them from the words of instruction, she may give them a taste of the solid food of the teachings.

John the Baptist preached a baptism of repentance, and all Judea went out to him. The Lord preaches a baptism of adoption—and who among those who have hoped in Him will not obey? That baptism was introductory; this one brings to completion. That one was a withdrawal from sin; this one is a kinship with God. John the Baptist's preaching was that of one man, and it drew everyone to repentance. But you—taught through the prophets, "Wash yourselves; become clean" (Isaiah 1:16); admonished through the psalms, "Come to Him, and be enlightened" (Psalm 34:6); evangelized through the apostles, "Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the promise of the Holy Spirit" (Acts 2:38); welcomed by the Lord Himself, who says, "Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28)—for all these readings have come together today—do you still hesitate, deliberate, and keep delaying?

You have been instructed in the word since infancy, and you have not yet committed yourself to the truth? Always learning, and you have not yet come to knowledge? A tester your whole life, a spy until old age—when will you become a Christian? When will we recognize you as one of us? Last year you were waiting for this present season; now you are waiting again for the next one.
